facts.fact: With Darrow's name first on the list the Confessors read out at the inn in Coldmere, Darrow believes it was written in a warm room in Calden by a man who has ridden knee to knee with him since they were boys, and hears again the words "Ride wide today."
facts.evidence: a man who had ridden knee to knee with him since they were boys had written his name first on the list

facts.fact: A list of the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's was read out at the inn in Coldmere; Hollis Garrow is second on it, and when Hollis asked who was first, Wren did not answer and looked at Darrow.

From the infirmary window he knew the cart standing at the winch-house at the foot of the Steps, shafts up and two oxen in the snow, as the one he had ridden the last of the Holloway in, and he had not forgotten the one thing its driver said to him.

At the infirmary window the Reckoning showed itself to him for the first time, a pale gold script hanging over his palms that he could read though nobody had learned it in three hundred years, and behind his own numbers stood fainter ones whose owner he did not need to be told.
facts.evidence: He could read it anyway, and it was reading him

facts.fact: To him, kneeling anew at a stone in front of a crowd would say aloud that the Grace left the Ninth because the Ninth failed it, and that forty-one men died at Harrow Ford for their own bad faith.
facts.evidence: for their own bad faith

facts.fact: He knew the grey cloaks and the smoking censer on the Holloway for Confessors before anyone else said the word, and his face went the color of the window.
facts.evidence: his face had gone the color of the window

facts.fact: His name is second on the list of the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's that was read out at the inn in Coldmere; asked who was first, Wren did not answer and looked at Darrow.
By Wren Ashdown's ledger at the head of the chapter, the captain of the Ninth has asked fourteen times whether he may go down the Steps, and Mender Vorne has said no fourteen times.
Asked how many Bindings she has done, she said only that it was enough to know what the soft season looks like, and agreed that was not a number.
facts.evidence: Enough to know what the soft season looks like

facts.fact: When Darrow saw the script of light above his palms, she did not look surprised; she said "So it's begun" and told him to close the door.
facts.evidence: She didn't look surprised. That frightened him more than the light had.

facts.fact: By the time Wren Ashdown reached the infirmary hall with word of the grey cloaks on the Holloway, Mother Ione had been told.
facts.evidence: Mother Ione's been told.

facts.fact: By Wren's account she was in the taproom at the inn in Coldmere with the House's salt on her cart when the Confessors' list was read out, and heard every name.
She drove the Holloway in the dark ahead of the grey cloaks, came up the Steps before the bell, and told the winch-brothers, who told the kitchen.

Her cart stands at the winch-house at the foot of the Steps with its shafts up and two oxen in the snow; Darrow knew it from the infirmary window as the cart he had ridden the last of the Holloway in.
Wren's ledger counts one cart at the winch-house, Thorne's, and one load waiting on the cage.
Her glass is in the bell tower of Saint Ysolde's; it was through Sister Pell's glass that Wren saw the riders on the Holloway.
What the glass showed: six riders and a cart on the Holloway, grey cloaks, and a censer smoking in the snow, which Hollis named Confessors.

Her ledger entry at the head of Chapter 1 records the Steps, the cots and how many are full, the day's bells, and the number of times the captain of the Ninth has asked to go down the Steps against the number of times Mender Vorne has refused him.
She told Darrow that Maelis says 'Time makes it possible, proof makes it permitted' in her sleep; Maelis says she does not sleep and that Wren lies, which Wren calls embellishing.
facts.evidence: and Wren lies

facts.fact: She came to the infirmary from the bell tower, where Sister Pell's glass had shown riders on the Holloway.

She brought the infirmary hall the news of six grey-cloaked riders and a cart on the Holloway, with a censer smoking in the snow, expected at the foot of the Steps by tomorrow night if the snow holds off.
She knows who stands second on the list of the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's that was read out at the inn in Coldmere: Hollis. When he asked who was first, she answered only by looking at Darrow.
facts.evidence: Wren didn't answer. She didn't have to. She was already looking at Darrow.

facts.fact: She brought word that Rae Thorne had heard the list read in the taproom at Coldmere, driven the Holloway in the dark ahead of the grey cloaks, and climbed the Steps before the bell to tell the winch-brothers.
Her ledger at the head of Chapter 1 also counts one cart at the winch-house, Thorne's, and one load waiting on the cage.
Bringing the news of the list, she said the named would be taken down the Steps, down the Holloway, all the way to the Oathspire, to kneel in front of whoever turns out to watch.
facts.evidence: all the way to the Oathspire

facts.fact: He is of Hollis Garrow's own Sixth Lance, not yet thirty, and has the cot next to Hollis's in the infirmary hall of Saint Ysolde's.
A boar spear went through his shoulder at the ford, and a fever followed; the shoulder is wrapped like a parcel.
He says his oath at every bell, and says he still feels a warmth in his chest.
facts.evidence: the eyes of a man who still felt a warmth in his chest, or said he did

facts.fact: He asked Hollis what it meant to be second on the list and whether they would take him down, and was told that nobody was taking anyone up eleven hundred steps in the snow.
He told Hollis that if the Confessors did come up he could kneel, that the heralds had said it was mercy and only kneeling, and that he would carry Hollis down the Steps himself if they let him.
Told to say his oath and shut his eyes, he shut them and his lips began to move, and he did not see where Hollis put the folded paper from his shirt.
facts.evidence: Orrin saw what he was told to see; he always had.

quote.text: I'd carry you down the Steps myself, if they'd let me.

facts.fact: While Hollis hid the writ, the Captain was shut in a cell down the hall with Mender Vorne and nothing came through the door; Hollis has thought for a fortnight that a man could fight sitting down, if somebody taught him to stop looking at the floor.

He can say the order from Harrow Ford with his eyes shut, and has kept the paper folded small inside his shirt, wax inward, against his ribs; he has not looked at the seal since he broke it on the west bank.
facts.evidence: wax inward, against his ribs

facts.fact: The lay brothers made him a leg of beech and a leather cup, which fits the way a boot fits someone else; he took nine steps on it and swore at every one.
He has not had a drink in two days, meant to tell somebody, and could not think who.
facts.evidence: He had not had a drink in two days, which he had meant to tell somebody and couldn't think who.

facts.fact: When Benedek Orrin of his own Sixth asked what second on the list meant and whether they would take him down, he said nobody was taking anyone up eleven hundred steps in the snow, and that they would read their list at the bottom and freeze.
For a fortnight he has thought of the Captain with a sword and a chair under him: a man could fight sitting down, if somebody taught him to stop looking at the floor.
facts.evidence: a man could fight sitting down, if somebody taught him to stop looking at the floor

facts.fact: He told Benedek to say his oath and shut his eyes, and while the lad's lips moved he pushed the folded writ, still unread, into the cup of the wooden leg, where no Confessor would think to look; he has been telling himself since midsummer that he will look at the wax later.
She was shut in a cell down the hall with the Captain while Hollis hid the writ; nothing came through the door, and at the end of the Interlude a latch lifted and it opened.

Behind the cell door, Maelis told him of two fires a man can carry: one poured in, which the hand that poured it can take back, and one built by his own work, which cannot be poured or taken; the script he saw counts only the built one.
He knew the name of the burned order before she said it, from the curse the lowlands make of it, and she forbade him to say it in the hall, to Wren, to the Prior, or to Hollis most of all.
facts.evidence: The Emberwardens.

facts.fact: He argued that Hollis, second on the list and lying on his back when it is read, was owed the knowing of the built fire before he was; Maelis answered that Hollis is owed a leg and will get a wooden one. When she asked what he would tell Hollis, he chose the answer himself: that she had started charging by the warning.
facts.evidence: I'll tell him you've started charging by the warning.

facts.fact: Maelis told him the Confessors do not need him to tell them anything: any Confessor who lays a hand on his knee will know what is in it, and the Crown has burned every hand it ever caught putting it there.
facts.evidence: Any Confessor who lays a hand on it will know what's in it

facts.fact: In her cell she told Darrow there are two fires a man can carry, one poured in and one built, that the script reads only what is one's own, and that no one full of Grace has ever seen it.

She named the order that lived by the built fire, burned by the Crown three hundred years ago, and forbade Darrow to speak of it in the hall, to Wren, the Prior, or Hollis most of all, because Hollis is second on a list and she wants his honest answer to be nothing.
Asked how she knows all this, she said only that she is a Mender and Menders remember things.
facts.evidence: I'm a Mender. We remember things.

facts.fact: When Darrow argued that Hollis was owed the knowing of the built fire, she said Hollis is owed a leg and will get a wooden one, that a Confessor watches a man's mouth while he answers, that Hollis must be able to answer with nothing and mean it, and that when he asks, Darrow will lie to him.
facts.evidence: Let Hollis answer with nothing and mean it

facts.fact: Behind the cell door she told Darrow that the Confessors don't need him to tell them anything, they need to see the knee: any Confessor who lays a hand on it will know what's in it, and the Crown has burned every hand it ever caught putting it there.
facts.evidence: the Crown has burned every hand it ever caught putting it there

facts.fact: He told the Captain the Grace forgives: kneel, and it comes back. Asked why mercy needs a list, he had no answer and apologised for not having one.
facts.evidence: Benedek had no answer, and apologised for not having one.

facts.fact: He asked Hollis and Benedek why the Confessors chase the Faithless up a mountain if the Grace left them for faithlessness, and why mercy needs a list with his name first; he kept what Maelis told him behind his teeth.

His read of the Confessors: a captain who won't kneel is a song in every taproom from the Steps to Calden, so they take the song down the mountain and make it kneel where people can see. "Mercy's the word on the paper. The paper's the point."
facts.evidence: Mercy's the word on the paper. The paper's the point.

facts.fact: Asked what the Grace did, he told Maelis: it made the river a road and every ache go quiet, and when it went it was cold, frost on his mail in midsummer. Asked whether he broke his oath, he said no.

He told Maelis the Grace did not go but was taken, since sixty men do not lose a thing in the same heartbeat by accident; she agreed that then somebody took it, and said that what it did at the ford, and whose doing, she does not know.
facts.evidence: Sixty men don't lose a thing in the same heartbeat by accident

facts.fact: Of the Grace: she has had her fingers on knees that carried it for twenty years; it holds things up, it doesn't mend them, and a man can run on a torn thing a long while with it under him and never know. Of Faithless: a word for a knight the Grace has left, which says it left because of him.
facts.evidence: It holds things up, Captain. It doesn't mend them.

facts.fact: Told the Grace was taken rather than lost, she agreed that then somebody took it, a finding and not a side, and said she was up here that day with her hands in another man's leg: what it did at the ford, and whose doing, she does not know.
facts.evidence: What it did at the ford, and whose doing, I don't know

facts.fact: At Mother Ione's council he saw Sister Pell's cup chatter on the hearth before it settled, and read it before he meant to, the way he read a line before a charge; nobody else looked.
facts.evidence: He read it before he meant to, the way he read a line before a charge. Nobody else looked.

facts.fact: Asked by Rae Thorne on the stair whether he rode a grey at the ford, he said yes and asked why; she did not say. He has not said Thistle's name since the river.
facts.evidence: He had not said her name since

facts.fact: At the council he asked to be put on the cage with the next load down before the grey cloaks reached the foot of the Steps, so the list would have nothing to climb for. Maelis answered for the fifteenth time, to the fire: the thread is soft, eleven hundred steps down are eleven hundred chances to tear it, and the cage is for salt. Rae said that down is where they are.
facts.evidence: the cage is for salt

facts.fact: At the Prior's council she gave the law: while Old Mercy rings at dawn and dusk, no blade climbs the Steps or passes the gate, and no name under it is taken down against its will; miss one ringing and the law lapses till the next.
facts.evidence: no name under it is taken down against its will

facts.fact: When Darrow asked the council to send him down on the cage before the grey cloaks came, she answered for the fifteenth time, to the fire and without looking round, that the answer is the same as the other fourteen and will be the same at fifty: the thread is soft, eleven hundred steps down are eleven hundred chances to tear it, and the cage is for salt.
facts.evidence: Fifteen, Captain, and the answer's the same as the other fourteen

facts.fact: When Darrow asked the council to send him down on the cage, she said that if he reached the bottom whole they would put him on his knees on a stone, the thread would go, and she does not do this twice.
facts.evidence: they put you on your knees on a stone

facts.fact: She holds her council in the warming room off the cloister, has the one good chair by the fire, and offers it to nobody.

She asked Rae Thorne how the list was read, had Maelis give Darrow the law of Old Mercy, and asked Sister Pell whether she would ring it dawn and dusk for as long as the grey cloaks care to sit at the bottom.

She has not yet decided whether Old Mercy rings. She called Darrow back from the stair to ask what he would have her know first, and what the lay brothers should tell the valley when it asks who sleeps up here.
facts.evidence: Before I decide whether Old Mercy rings, is there anything you'd have me know?

facts.fact: She let the Captain ask to be sent down and the Mender answer him, then closed the council having heard them all: Sister Pell would hear from her before dusk, and the lay brothers would want to know what to say to the valley.
facts.evidence: you'll hear from me before dusk

facts.fact: At her council she put it to Darrow as a question: if the lay brothers tell the valley there's nobody up here, what does a sanctuary bell tell it at dusk? After his answer, Old Mercy did not ring at dusk, nor at the next dawn.
facts.evidence: what does a sanctuary bell tell it at dusk?

facts.fact: When Darrow offered to go down on the cage so the list would have nothing to climb for, she asked him how many names the next writ would carry once the House had given them one, and did not wait for him to count.
facts.evidence: how many will the next writ carry?

facts.fact: At Mother Ione's council she said the list was read slow, so the room could count; and the room counted.
facts.evidence: So the room could count

facts.fact: On the stair after the council she stopped one step above Darrow, eye to eye, and asked whether he rode a grey at the ford. When he said yes and asked why, she went on up without answering; the bell at her belt rang once at the turn.
facts.evidence: went on up without answering

facts.fact: When Darrow asked to be sent down the Steps before the grey cloaks came, she said from the door that down is where they are: the first thing she had said in the council that was not an answer.
facts.evidence: Down's where they are

facts.fact: At the council, after saying down is where they are, she said she has carted men down to kneel since midsummer and has not carted one back up.
facts.evidence: I've not carted one back up.

facts.fact: She has rung the House's bells for fifty years.
Old Mercy rings only when the House is keeping somebody, dawn and dusk till they are gone; once it has been rung, she says, the law has lapsed twice, both times for snow, and not on her rope.
facts.evidence: Not on my rope

facts.fact: She watches the speaker's mouth, not their eyes; when she set her cup on the hearth it chattered twice on the stone before it settled.
facts.evidence: the cup chatter twice before it settled

people.did: Wrapped in two shawls by the fire at Mother Ione's council, watching the Prior's mouth; saying that once Old Mercy is rung the law has lapsed twice, both for snow, never on her rope, and that she will ring Old Mercy as long as it takes.
people.now: Keeper of the House's bells. Asked by Mother Ione whether she would ring Old Mercy every dawn and every dusk for as long as the grey cloaks care to sit at the foot of the Steps, she said she had rung the bells fifty years and the Prior could ask the bell if it was tired. When the grey cloaks were at the bars and Wren ran for the tower, Old Mercy rang late and dragging, after two of them were already through the wicket, and Wren came back with Pell's slowness in her face. The Confessor told the Prior she keeps a fine bell, a little slow on the rope.

quote.text: Fifty years I've rung the bells. Ask the bell if it's tired.

story_so_far.sister-pell: Her glass in the bell tower is where the grey cloaks were first seen on the Holloway. At Mother Ione's council in the warming room she sat by the fire in two shawls and said Old Mercy rings only when the House is keeping somebody, and once rung the law has lapsed twice, both for snow, never on her rope; asked whether she would ring Old Mercy dawn and dusk for as long as the grey cloaks wait, she said she had rung the bells fifty years, and the Prior could ask the bell if it was tired.

facts.fact: While the two captains played knucklebones he lay on the far side of Hollis's cot, and his lips began to move for his oath before either of them had heard the bell coming.
facts.evidence: Benedek's lips had begun to move

facts.fact: Back from the council he read Hollis's hands as he had read Sister Pell's cup, asked once about them, was put off, and played him at knucklebones for a story told true; he caught the stone on the back of his hand, and Hollis paid: two days without a drink, three by the dusk bell.
facts.evidence: The bone sat on Darrow's knuckles

facts.fact: His answer, when Hollis said he had not known who to tell: that he had told the one man on the mountain who could not buy him a drink.
facts.evidence: the one man on this mountain who can't buy you a drink

facts.fact: He had the knucklebones out, five sheep's knuckles on the blanket, and played Darrow for a story told true; when Darrow caught the stone he chanted the loser's lines and paid: two days without a drink, three by the dusk bell, and he had meant to tell somebody and couldn't think who.
facts.evidence: I meant to tell somebody, and I couldn't think who.

facts.fact: His hand under the falling bones was steady the way a thing is steady when it is being held still; when Darrow asked about his hands he called them a wonder of the age and told him to sit down or play.
facts.evidence: steady the way a thing is steady when it is being held still

facts.fact: At the hour bell he asked the Captain to say the oath with him, only the words, since he cannot stand for it and the Captain cannot kneel; he said the Captain needn't, and that it is easier, two.
facts.evidence: Would you say it with me? Only the words.

facts.fact: He was not listening for the Captain's voice; he watched his mouth, and what he needed was the shape of the words beside his own. When they finished together he let his breath out and thanked the Captain to the roof.
facts.evidence: Thank you, Captain

facts.fact: Asked by Benedek to say the oath with him at the hour bell, only the words, he said go on, then; he had first said them kneeling in a cold chapel with Aldric Vane's shoulder against his and had not said them since the river, and they were still in him whole, by heart, and no use to anyone.
facts.evidence: whole, by heart, and no use to anyone

facts.fact: His lips moved with Benedek's and no sound came out of him; the lad was watching his mouth, not listening for his voice, and when they finished nothing came up through Darrow's hand, there being no stone under it.
facts.evidence: Darrow's lips moved with his

facts.fact: When the bell came and Benedek asked the Captain for the words, he shut his eyes on the instant, the way forty years of barracks teach a man to be asleep when something is about to be asked of him; afterwards he opened one eye, looked at Darrow for the length of a heartbeat, and shut it again.
facts.evidence: opened one eye

facts.fact: At the dawn bell, as his lips began to move, his eyes went past Hollis to the Captain's mouth and waited there until it moved with his.
facts.evidence: waited there until it moved with his

facts.fact: At the dawn bell his lips moved with Benedek's oath again, with Benedek watching his mouth.
facts.evidence: waited there until it moved with his

facts.fact: Asked by the Prior whether he told the valley story for the House or for the river, he said the river had had enough of them.
facts.evidence: The river's had enough of us.

facts.fact: The Prior asked him, because he reads a line before it moves, to tell Wren when, once the grey cloaks are at the bars; he said he would.
facts.evidence: You read a line before it moves

facts.fact: The low wall-walk beside the gate can be reached from the court without a stair, which is the whole of Maelis's reason for allowing him on it.
facts.evidence: the whole of Maelis's reason for allowing it

facts.fact: Through Pell's glass he read the grey cloaks' line: five strung along the last of the Holloway, their cart in the middle, and at the head a man whose saddle-bow trailed the censer's smoke.
facts.evidence: at the head a man whose saddle-bow trailed the censer's smoke

facts.fact: He told Rae Thorne to go down while the grey cloaks were an hour out and be on the road to Coldmere by dark; when she had let the road shut, he said her name and told her that had been her road.
facts.evidence: That was your road.

facts.fact: He told Rae Thorne he had asked fifteen times to go down those steps and she could walk down them today; it came out harder than he meant it to.
facts.evidence: Fifteen times I've asked to go down those steps.

facts.fact: When the Prior told him there would be no law on the gate till Old Mercy rang, he had slept like a stone, and did not say so.
facts.evidence: He had slept like a stone.

facts.fact: At the dawn bell he lay on his back between Benedek and the Captain while they said the words and studied the beams; whatever he made of it, he kept in his beard.
facts.evidence: Whatever he made of it, he kept in his beard.

facts.fact: She came up the hall on the last stroke of the dawn bell and waited at the foot of Darrow's cot until Benedek's lips stopped moving before she spoke.
facts.evidence: She waited until they stopped.

facts.fact: At first light the winch-brothers went down with Darrow's story of the far side of the mountain, to tell it at the winch-house fire, so that the valley would have it by noon.
facts.evidence: with your far side of the mountain

facts.fact: She asked Darrow whether he told it for the House or for the river; he said the river had had enough of them.
facts.evidence: or for the river?

facts.fact: At the next dawn she told Darrow Old Mercy had not rung at dusk, so the valley heard what it always hears from the House; when he said there was no law on the gate, she said not till she rings, and asked whether he had slept any worse for it.
facts.evidence: Did you sleep any worse for it?

facts.fact: She asked Darrow, who reads a line before it moves, to tell Wren when, once the grey cloaks are at the bars; it was not a question, and he said he would.
facts.evidence: will you tell Wren when?

facts.fact: From the gate wall at noon, through Sister Pell's glass, Darrow watched a grey cloak walk round her cart at the winch-house, climb onto the box and put his boots up on the board; she had not asked for the glass.

Darrow told her to go down while the rest of the grey cloaks were an hour out, ask the man off her box and be on the road to Coldmere by dark, and that once they had the cage she would be up there till the thaw; she said "Aye" to all of it. When he said he had asked fifteen times to go down those steps and she could walk down them today, she did not say aye.
facts.evidence: She did not say aye to that.

facts.fact: When the five were in at the winch-house she pinned her cloak at the throat with its iron clasp and drew up her hood; when Darrow said that had been her road, she said the first two names on that list rode up in her cart.
facts.evidence: The first two names on that list rode up in my cart.

quote.text: The first two names on that list rode up in my cart.

facts.fact: She lent Wren her glass counted out, one glass, two caps and one strap, to be counted back by the next bell.
facts.evidence: Counted out. One glass, two caps, one strap

facts.fact: Sister Pell lent her the glass counted out, one glass, two caps and one strap, to be counted back by the next bell.
facts.evidence: One glass, two caps, one strap

facts.fact: From the gate wall at noon she counted six riders, one cart and one censer, with one of the six already off the road: three bells early, because the snow held off.
facts.evidence: Three bells early. The snow held off.

facts.fact: When the five came in at the winch-house she lowered the glass and, for once, had no number for it.
facts.evidence: for once, had no number for it

facts.fact: On the wall after the grey cloaks came in, he stood until the knee went from stiff to sullen and shifted off it twice, which he did not think anyone had seen; when Rae sat on the gate-ward's bench, he sat at the other end before he had decided to.
facts.evidence: He sat at the other end before he had decided to.

facts.fact: Her oxen have names; asked to tell Darrow them, she said they know them.
facts.evidence: They know them.

facts.fact: Reminded that Hollis cursed everything on the road the day she drove him, she said he did the oxen before her, and something came and went at the corner of her mouth that was for the oxen.
facts.evidence: He did the oxen before me.

facts.fact: Of her oxen at the winch-house with a grey cloak on her cart: they'll stand; a mule won't stand at the winch-house, and an ox will stand all winter.
facts.evidence: An ox'll stand all winter.

facts.fact: When Darrow's knee began to shake from the standing, she sat down at one end of the gate-ward's bench, and he sat at the other before he had decided to; then she said, once, to the valley, that his leg was shaking.
facts.evidence: Leg was shaking

facts.fact: He asked Rae Thorne why she had asked whether he rode a grey; she said carters look at horses, which he took for true and standing in front of another thing.
facts.evidence: true and still be standing in front of another thing

facts.fact: The mare's name came as far as his teeth and stopped; saying it would mean asking what a carter had seen of a grey and hearing the answer, and he did not say it on the wall.
facts.evidence: The mare's name came as far as his teeth and stopped there.

facts.fact: Asked on the gate wall why she had asked whether he rode a grey at the ford, she said, to the valley, that carters look at horses; Darrow saw her hands, between her knees, close on each other.
facts.evidence: Carters look at horses.

facts.fact: She left the bench on the first stroke of the hour bell, and at the turn of the walk stopped and said that the near one of her oxen is the slow one.
facts.evidence: The near one's the slow one

facts.fact: At the gate he stood among the wounded who could walk, at the foot of the gatehouse stair with his back to its post, where a man could lean without seeming to; nobody in grey looked at him when his name was read first.
facts.evidence: Nobody in grey looked at him.

facts.fact: When his name was read his weight came off the post: a flinch that Wren felt through his sleeve and Hollis saw from the window, and nobody else.
facts.evidence: His weight came off the post.

facts.fact: The Prior had asked him at the dawn bell to tell Wren when to have Old Mercy rung, once the grey cloaks stopped wanting to read and started wanting to come in; the bell could not ring until the light was off the bars, and she meant it not to ring at all if paper was all they had brought.
facts.evidence: the Prior meant it not to ring at all if paper was all they had brought

facts.fact: He watched the Confessor's hands and the four men behind him, and the script, which until then had only ever read him, came up over his palms unasked and read the man at the bars: a fire all of it poured, and under the pouring nothing of his own; there was no lie in him, and the wicket was already open in his mind. Darrow said, 'Wren. Now.'
facts.evidence: Until that moment it had only ever read him.

facts.fact: He took the three strides to the wicket and put his shoulder to it beside the gate-ward's to shut it on a third grey cloak; the man leaned, the wicket threw Darrow off it against the gate, and the knee, deep in where the thread was, said one thing, quite clearly. Lay brothers and Rae Thorne shut it.
facts.evidence: said one thing, quite clearly

facts.fact: Going back to his post among the wounded, he passed the two grey cloaks who had come through the wicket close enough to touch, and neither of them looked at him twice.
facts.evidence: Neither of them looked at him twice.

facts.fact: Marrant called for him by name and rank to the whole court, as a man says a name he is sure of: come down and kneel, and the rest of the paper goes back into his cloak; he would wait.
facts.evidence: as a man says a name he is sure of

facts.fact: The Confessors had his name and had never seen his face; among eleven wounded men in infirmary shirts at the gate, it was one more.
facts.evidence: None of them had ever seen his face

facts.fact: Two lay brothers carried him up the gatehouse's inside stair in a chair to the window, because he had said, loud enough for the court, that he would see the man who wanted him.
facts.evidence: he would see the man who wanted him

facts.fact: When the Captain's name was read first he made a sound in his beard that was not a word.

facts.fact: When Marrant read his name second he looked at the blue wax of the seal against the bars and held there, then away to the mountain, and said nothing at all, which was not like him; his hands on the sill were steady because he was holding them so.
facts.evidence: They were steady because he was holding them so.

facts.fact: He came to the bars with four grey cloaks in the hour before dusk; the sixth of them had stayed at the winch-house with his boots on Rae Thorne's cart.
facts.evidence: Five came to the bars.

facts.fact: He named himself to the Prior as Ivo Marrant, Confessor, under the Knight-Confessor's seal, as if they had corresponded.
facts.evidence: as if they had corresponded

facts.fact: He had been told at the winch-house fire that the Faithless of Harrow Ford went down the far side a week since, and read anyway: he has read to empty beds before, he said, and finds it steadies the hand.
facts.evidence: I find it steadies the hand.

facts.fact: He unrolled the writ against the bars so the court could see its seal, blue wax the size of a child's palm, and read Darrow's name first and Hollis's second, then the Ninth's names and the Sixth's, slow, so the court could count.

facts.fact: He did not read the far cots, and said so himself: the Crown has no quarrel with men who can't answer.

facts.fact: He held the writ out for the wicket under the law of guests, as a courier's paper, and when the Prior made him wait he said he would hate to tell the bell-houses her House broke one old law to keep a courier standing in the cold; when the wicket opened a hand's width, two of his men came through it and a third held it open.
facts.evidence: I'd hate to tell the bell-houses

facts.fact: What Darrow read in him at the bars: a fire, all of it poured, and under the pouring nothing of his own; no lie in him, and the wicket already open in his mind.

facts.fact: When Old Mercy rang and the Prior spoke the law of names, his eyes went past her shoulder to Maelis and stayed there a beat longer than courtesy, and his smile changed its weight.
facts.evidence: a beat longer than courtesy

facts.fact: He told the Prior she keeps a fine bell, a little slow on the rope, called his two men back out through the wicket, and said the grey below the gate where the springs steam is the law's ground and nobody's: they would make their fire on the lower terrace, and bells grow tired.
facts.evidence: A little slow on the rope.

facts.fact: He called for Ser Darrow by name to the whole court, as a man says a name he is sure of: come down and kneel, and the rest of the paper goes back into his cloak and never comes out; he would wait, it is the thing he is best at.
facts.evidence: It's the thing I'm best at.

facts.fact: She stood a pace behind Mother Ione's shoulder at the gate while the Confessor read; when his eyes went past the Prior to her and stayed a beat longer than courtesy, she looked back at him with the pipe clamped and nothing in her face at all.
facts.evidence: nothing in her face at all

facts.fact: She ordered nobody into the court; at the hour bell she asked whether the House would like to see who had climbed so far to read to it, and the House came.

facts.fact: She stood before the gate with Maelis a pace behind her shoulder; when the Confessor said she would forgive him if he read anyway, she asked, 'Would I stop you?'

facts.fact: She let the Confessor hold his paper out through the bars while the bell did not come; when he said he would hate to tell the bell-houses her House broke the law of guests to keep a courier standing in the cold, she asked the gate-ward whether they should take the Confessor's paper.

facts.fact: When Old Mercy rang she told the Confessor, without moving and lowering her voice so the court leaned to hear, that while it rings no blade climbs the Steps or passes the gate, and the other half, which his order reads at every bell-house twice over: no name under it is taken down against its will.

facts.fact: At the reading she stood at the end of the lay brothers' line in the court, as still as anything she had ever driven.

facts.fact: When a third grey cloak held the wicket open and it threw Darrow off, her shoulder went in under the gate-ward's, set as she would set it to a cart gone into a rut, and the wicket shut on the man's arm.

facts.fact: When Wren ran for the tower, Old Mercy came up out of it late and dragging, as if the rope had argued with the hands that found it, after two grey cloaks were already through the wicket; Wren came back with Pell's slowness in her face.

facts.fact: In the court she stood at Darrow's left with her ledger against her chest and no pencil behind her ear, because she was not there to count; when his name was read her hand closed on his sleeve and stayed there.

facts.fact: At 'Wren. Now.' she was gone along the inner wall toward the tower before the word was finished, and the ledger went with her.

facts.fact: She came back from the tower with Pell's slowness in her face and took her place at Darrow's left again, and for the second time that day had no number for a thing.

title: Darrow of Edgemoor

facts.fact: He crossed the court to the gate with the whole House watching and nobody stopping him, put his hand on the bars, and called the Confessor back from the head of the Steps by both his names.
facts.evidence: Darrow put his hand on the bars.

facts.fact: He gave his own name and rank through the bars, Darrow of Edgemoor, Captain of the Ninth, and told the Confessor he had read to a full bed: nobody went down the far side, and nobody is going down this one.
facts.evidence: You've read to a full bed.

facts.fact: Marrant came back to the bars and looked at his face, the first time anyone in grey had, called him Captain, and thanked the Prior for her candour.

facts.fact: The Prior, who had heard her House's story die at her own gate, did not reproach him; she asked whether the shoulder was hurt.
facts.evidence: She asked him whether the shoulder was hurt.

facts.fact: From the window Hollis told him he had moved when his name was read, that he had seen it and nobody else had, and that he had walked up and given it anyway; Darrow did not ask him how he was.

facts.fact: Maelis looked at the knee first and then at his face, and told him that hidden he was a lie they'd have found by the thaw, and named he is a law they'll have to break where the valley can watch; the knee lies to her every morning, he hadn't, and he was to keep it that way. She sent him to the hall slowly and said she would read the knee tonight.

facts.fact: Before he went to the bars he weighed it: the grey cloaks had walked the wounded looking at faces, and next time it would be every cot in the hall and eleven sore men taking his share of it; the lie had died when the Confessor said the beds weren't empty, and the bell had already told the valley the House had someone. It might as well have a name.
facts.evidence: It might as well have a name.

facts.fact: When the Captain had given his name at the bars, Hollis told him from the window that he had moved when his name was read, that he had seen it and nobody else had, and that he had walked up and given it anyway; then he said 'Captain', once, and let the word carry what it needed to.

facts.fact: Called back from the head of the Steps by both his names, he came to the bars and looked at the Captain's face, the first time anyone in grey had; told that he had read to a full bed, he paused the length of a man deciding to be pleased, called him Captain, and thanked the Prior for her candour.
facts.evidence: Mother Ione. Thank you for your candour.

people.did: Going down the first flight of the Steps into the dusk after the Captain of the Ninth gave his name at the bars; he had looked at Darrow's face, called him Captain, and thanked the Prior for her candour.
people.now: Camped on the lower terrace below the gate of Saint Ysolde's with four grey cloaks; the sixth of them keeps the winch-house. He read his list at the bars and was answered by Old Mercy and the law of names. Then the Captain of the Ninth crossed the court and gave his name at the bars; Marrant looked at his face, called him Captain, and thanked the Prior for her candour. He has said he will wait. That night his camp sat up in turns round one fire, where the whole House could see it, and a man of his at the bars sent the Captain of the Ninth the Confessor's good night, by his rank.

facts.fact: After the wicket she saw to the bloodied lay brother first, two fingers under his jaw, and asked after his teeth; then she came to Darrow, looked at the knee first and then at his face, and took the pipe out to say that hidden he was a lie they'd have found by the thaw, and named he is a law they'll have to break where the valley can watch; the knee lies to her every morning, he hadn't, and he was to keep it that way. She sent him to the hall slowly and said she would read the knee tonight.

facts.fact: When Darrow had given his name at the bars she was rubbing the shoulder she had put to the wicket and watching him the way she had watched the valley from the wall.

story_so_far.ivo-marrant: He led the grey cloaks up the Holloway and the Thousand Steps and came to the gate of Saint Ysolde's in the hour before dusk, five at the bars and the sixth at the winch-house, with the censer in his own hand. He had been told at the winch-house fire that the Faithless had gone down the far side a week since, and read his list anyway: he has read to empty beds before, he said, and finds it steadies the hand. He held his paper out for the wicket under the law of guests until the Prior could not refuse it without breaking that law; when the wicket opened a hand's width, two of his men came through, and Old Mercy rang late and stopped them a pace from the wounded. Mother Ione gave him the law's other half: no name under the bell is taken down against its will. He called her bell fine and a little slow on the rope, made his camp on the lower terrace, and called for the Captain of the Ninth to come down and kneel. The Captain came to the bars instead and gave his name; Marrant called him Captain and thanked the Prior for her candour.
story_so_far.rae-thorne: She drove the last cart of Darrow's road north, a salt-cart off the Holloway with its load left at the landing to make room for two knights and a leg that was not there, talking to her oxen the whole day and to her passengers not at all. When Hollis started on her she said 'Aye' as if he had remarked on the weather. At the foot of the Steps she looked at Darrow's leg once, the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel, rang the bell at her belt three times, and a bell answered from the cloud; the lay brothers who came down with the litter called her Rae, and the one thing she said to Darrow all day was that they would count him up and he should not help. Seven weeks after Darrow's Binding she was in the taproom at Coldmere with the House's salt on her cart when the Confessors read out their list of the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's. She drove the Holloway in the dark ahead of them, climbed the Steps before the bell, and told the winch-brothers, who told the kitchen; her cart and oxen wait at the winch-house below, at the foot of the Steps. When the grey cloaks came in three bells early and one of them put his boots up on her cart, she stood on the gate wall beside Darrow, said "Aye" to every reason he gave her to go, and let the road shut: the first two names on that list, she said, rode up in her cart. In the court at dusk she stood at the end of the lay brothers' line while the list was read, and when Darrow's shoulder could not shut the wicket on a third grey cloak, hers went in where his had been and it shut.

recap: At Harrow Ford the Grace went out of the Ninth Lance in mid-river, and only a thread of it came back; Darrow's knee gave way with no blade near it, and forty-one of his sixty did not come home. Carried up the Thousand Steps to Saint Ysolde's, he chose Maelis Vorne's Binding over kneeling again at the Oathspire.
